payload.title: Make session resume re-bind tmux window options on the current pane
payload.description: endless session resume execs 'claude --resume' in the current pane but never sets the tmux window options that task spawn sets (@endless_task_id, @endless_project_id, @endless_spawned_by), and relies on the hook's per-event self-heal for @endless_session_uuid. So a resumed pane lacks the window identity that _current_pane_task() (the E-1968 clobber guard, session_cmd.py:605) and session-status focal resolution read from @endless_task_id. Fix: on resume, set the window options on the current pane to match spawn. Long-standing gap since resume was introduced (eb2206ad), not a regression.
payload.text:
# Make `session resume` re-bind the tmux window options on the current pane

## Problem
`resume_session` (src/endless/session_cmd.py:558) resolves the target, then
`os.chdir(worktree)` + `os.execvp("claude", ["claude","--resume",uuid])`
(session_cmd.py:634-637). It sets NO tmux window options. So a pane resumed into
lacks the `@endless_*` window identity that a spawned window carries.

The four options and who sets them today:
- `@endless_task_id`, `@endless_project_id`, `@endless_spawned_by` — written ONLY
  by the spawn launcher (internal/spawnlaunchcmd/spawn_launch.go:39 ->
  tmux_driver.go:92-97). Never on the resume path.
- `@endless_session_uuid` — written by the hook every event
  (internal/hookcmd/claude.go:287, setTmuxSessionUUID), meant to self-heal.

## Why it matters
A resumed pane with no `@endless_task_id` silently loses:
- `_current_pane_task()` — the E-1968 clobber guard in resume itself
  (session_cmd.py:605) can't see the pane's held task.
- `session status` focal-task resolution, which reads the window's
  `@endless_task_id`.

## Fix
On the resume path, before `os.execvp`, set the window options on the current
pane to match a spawned window:
- `@endless_task_id` = resolved task id
- `@endless_project_id` = resolved project id
- `@endless_session_uuid` = resolved session uuid (set it here rather than
  depend on the hook's per-event self-heal, which is more fragile — see below)

Open design question for the implementer: `@endless_spawned_by` means "which
session spawned this window." A resumed pane was NOT spawned by `task spawn`, so
setting it is debatable — likely omit it (or record a resume-origin marker).
Decide during implementation; task_id/project_id/session_uuid are the clear wins.

## Not a regression
Verified via git pickaxe: `git log -S 'set -w' -- src/endless/session_cmd.py`
and `-S '@endless_task_id' -- …` both return zero commits. resume has been
option-less since it was introduced (eb2206ad). None of E-2074/E-2102/E-1918/
E-1851/E-1898/E-1976 touched the resume/hook option writes. This is a
long-standing design gap, not a recent breakage.

## Related but SEPARATE (do not fold in)
A distinct symptom was observed alongside this: `@endless_session_uuid` absent
even though the hook should self-heal it every event. That points at the hook
not reaching claude.go:287 for the affected session (candidates: the
`shouldSkipForWorktree` early return at claude.go:232, or a stale/missing
worktree-local hook wiring in that worktree's .claude/settings.json). That is a
hook-firing/wiring diagnostic, not confirmed as a code defect, and is NOT part
of this task. Setting session_uuid on the resume path (above) makes resume
robust to it regardless.

## Origin
Found while debugging a `session resume` in an unrelated session's worktree; the
task that session happened to be under (E-1834) is NOT related to this bug.

payload.title: Give the session state vocabulary an owning Go package
payload.description: Session state (working, idle, needs_input, ended) is spelled as string literals across ~70 non-test sites in Go, Python and SQL, with no owning package — the defect E-1891 fixed for task status, unfixed here. Build internal/sessionstate as its counterpart: members, labels, glyphs, five curated groups (All, Live, MayWrite, AwaitsHuman, DisplayOrder), SQLList, and a transition table naming which code writes each state. Expose it as 'endless-go session-state' and convert Python to a thin pass-through holding none of the vocabulary. Pure refactor: no state is added and behaviour is byte-identical. Also deletes the obsolete duplicate CREATE TABLE sessions in db.py, whose banned CHECK constraint is a fifth vocabulary site. Blocks E-2091, which adds a fifth state and must be a one-row change.
payload.text:
# Plan — an owning package for the session state vocabulary

Counterpart to `internal/taskstatus` (E-1891), same shape for the same reason.
Pure refactor: no state is added, no behaviour changes.

## 1. `internal/sessionstate`

A `Status` string type and the four members in lifecycle order: `Working`,
`Idle`, `NeedsInput`, `Ended`.

One `groups` map, five rows:

| Group          | Members (in order)                      | Consumer |
|----------------|-----------------------------------------|----------|
| `All`          | working, idle, needs_input, ended       | the vocabulary; validation |
| `Live`         | working, idle, needs_input              | the 29 `state != 'ended'` sites |
| `MayWrite`     | working, idle                           | `hookcmd.sessionMayWrite` |
| `AwaitsHuman`  | idle, needs_input                       | the board's attention ranking |
| `DisplayOrder` | working, needs_input, idle, ended       | `session list`'s sort CASE |

Accessors mirroring `taskstatus` exactly, so the two packages read alike:
`Get`, `Has`, `SQLList`, `Rank`, `Label`, `Glyph`, `Valid`, `Validate`,
`GroupSlug`, `ParseGroup`, `AllGroupSlugs`, `AllGroups`.

Glyphs move from `session_cmd.py` unchanged — `⟳` working, `‖` idle, `?`
needs_input, `␥` ended — plus `⁇` for a state not in the map, matching the
unknown-glyph idiom both existing views already use.

`Live` is the members list, not a negation. Call sites keep reading
`state IN (<Live>)` rather than `NOT IN ('ended')`, so a state added later is
classified rather than silently inheriting "live".

## 2. The transition table

`transitions.go`: rows of `{from, to, trigger}` where `trigger` names the hook
event and the helper that performs the write. Initial rows, from the writers
verified while planning:

| From    | To           | Trigger |
|---------|--------------|---------|
| (none)  | needs_input  | `SessionStart` → `monitor.InitSession` |
| (none)  | working      | `monitor.RegisterSession` / `TouchSession` INSERT |
| any     | working      | task claim → `monitor.BindSessionToTask` |
| any     | idle         | `Stop` → `monitor.IdleSession` |
| any     | ended        | `SessionEnd` → `monitor.EndSession`; the dedup sweep |
| ended   | needs_input  | any hook event → `monitor.TouchSession` revive (E-1686) |

A `Transitions()` accessor and a test pinning the table. The conversion pass in
§5 confirms each row against the site it names and adds any writer it finds;
that is mechanical discovery, not an open decision.

No mermaid, no generated doc, no drift check — see the analysis.

## 3. `endless-go session-state`

`internal/sessionstatecmd`, registered in `cmd/endless-go/main.go` beside
`task-status`, with the same verbs: `groups`, `get <group>`, `has <group>
<state>`, `sql-list <group>`, `rank <group> <state>`, `label <state>`,
`glyph <state>`, `transitions`. No DB access; the vocabulary is compile-time
data.

## 4. `src/endless/session_states.py`

A pass-through client modelled on `src/endless/statuses.py`, holding no
vocabulary and no group list — one-line shellouts that know verb names and
nothing else. Fails closed: if `endless-go` cannot be resolved or is too old to
know `session-state`, it says so and stops. There is no fallback to fall back to;
a hardcoded copy would be the duplicate this deletes.

`SESSION_STATES = get("all")` at module scope, mirroring `TASK_STATUSES`, so
`cli.py`'s `--state` choice is built from the registry.

## 5. The conversion

Go:
- `internal/monitor` — `session.go`, `live_sessions.go`, `session_notices.go`,
  `worktree_inuse.go`, `project_status.go`, and any other site the sweep finds.
- `internal/hookcmd/claude.go` — the local `stateWorking`/`stateIdle`/
  `stateNeedsInput` constants go; `sessionMayWrite` becomes
  `sessionstate.Has(sessionstate.MayWrite, s.State)`.
- `internal/events/executor.go` — the revive CASE.

Python:
- `cli.py` — `--state`'s `click.Choice` from `SESSION_STATES`.
- `session_cmd.py` — the icon map, the legend, and the sort `CASE`, the last
  built from `DisplayOrder`'s rank.

`internal/projectstatuscmd`'s `boardSessionStates` is deliberately NOT replaced
by a group. It is `'working','idle'` because E-1976 withholds the dead
`needs_input` placeholder, which is a temporary exclusion rather than a durable
meaning; E-2091 deletes it. It stays a documented local constant.

## 6. Verification

`.endless/tasks/e-<id>/verify.sh`, sourcing `_harness.sh`:

1. Fail-fast unit gate: the new package's tests, plus `internal/monitor`,
   `internal/hookcmd`, `internal/projectstatuscmd`, and the Python suite.
2. Group membership pinned exactly, in the idiom of
   `taskstatus`'s `TestGroupMembershipIsPinned` — a deliberate change edits the
   table and says so; an accidental one fails.
3. `MayWrite` is asserted to be what the declaration gate admits, so the gate's
   behaviour is pinned to the group rather than to a switch.
4. No session-state literal survives outside `internal/sessionstate` and the
   schema: a sweep over Go, Python and SQL, excluding the package itself,
   comments, and `boardSessionStates`.
5. Python holds no vocabulary: an AST check that `session_states.py` imports no
   `db`/`sqlite3` and declares no state list, and that `session_cmd.py` and
   `cli.py` no longer carry literals.
6. Byte-identical behaviour, which is the point of the task being a pure
   refactor: against a seeded throwaway database, `endless session list` and
   `endless session list --json` render the same rows, glyphs, legend and sort
   order as the pinned expectations captured from the pre-change build.

## 7. Folded in, per ED-1550 rule 2

`src/endless/db.py` carries a second `CREATE TABLE sessions` with
`CHECK (state IN ('working','idle','needs_input','ended'))` — a fifth vocabulary
site, on a table shape missing `process_id`, `epic_id`, `hidden` and the
`report_*` columns the authoritative `internal/schema/schema.sql` defines.

CHECK constraints are banned (`internal/schema/schema.sql`'s header: SQLite
cannot ALTER or DROP one without rebuilding the whole table, which caused
catastrophic data loss; validation lives in application code — see also
ED-1495). The block is guarded by `if not _has_table(conn, "sessions")` and the
Go schema runs on every connection, so it is unreachable as well as wrong.

Mike's call (2026-09-01): delete it here rather than update it. It is evidence
folded into an open task, not a new filing.

## 8. Not in scope

- No fifth state. E-2091 adds `prompted`, and this task exists to make that a
  one-row change.
- No generated lifecycle diagram or drift check.
- No change to `sessions.state` values in the database, and no migration.
- No change to what any state MEANS. Where a group's membership encodes a rule
  that reads oddly — `AwaitsHuman` including `idle` — the rule is preserved as
  found and the reading is left to E-2091.
payload.analysis:
## The defect

`sessions.state` carries four values — `working`, `idle`, `needs_input`, `ended`
— and nothing owns them. They are spelled as string literals across roughly 70
non-test sites in three languages: Go (`internal/monitor`, `internal/hookcmd`,
`internal/projectstatuscmd`), Python (`src/endless/cli.py`,
`src/endless/session_cmd.py`), and SQL embedded in both.

This is precisely the defect E-1891 fixed for task status, left unfixed here.
`src/endless/statuses.py` records what it cost there: status lived as bare
literals across ~20 sites in two languages, and twice — E-1648's `submitted`,
E-1845's `untriaged` — a status was added and a site was missed.

Measured distribution of the SQL predicates:

- `state != 'ended'` — 29 sites. By an order of magnitude the most common thing
  anyone asks about a session.
- `state = 'ended'` — 21 sites.
- single-state reads and writes — the remainder.

## What made it urgent

E-1976 added a project attention board whose loudest rank is "a session is
waiting on you". Building its follow-up (E-2091) I proposed routing Claude
Code's permission-prompt Notification to `needs_input`, on the evidence that no
live transition ever writes that state.

That was wrong in a way a grep does not reveal. `needs_input` is enforced:
`hookcmd.sessionMayWrite` refuses file writes from a session in that state under
`enforce` tracking, with the message "you asked your user something and the
answer has not arrived. There is no command for you to run." Routing permission
prompts there would have refused the session's next write after the user
approved.

The failure is structural, not a lapse of care. The gate's admission set is a Go
`switch` with a silent `default: return false`. A new state joins the refused set
by default and says nothing. Nothing in the code makes adding a state a decision
about whether it may write.

## Why groups, and why these five

Each of the five is a predicate already in the tree, not a speculation. `Live`
retires the 29-site majority. `MayWrite` is the one that pays for the exercise:
once the gate reads a named group, a state cannot be added without someone
classifying it, which is the forcing function that would have caught the
collision above. `AwaitsHuman` is the group the board's attention rank expresses,
and drawing it now is what keeps E-2091 to one row. `DisplayOrder` and `All`
carry `session list`'s sort and the vocabulary itself.

This follows `internal/taskstatus`'s governing property: adding a Group is one
row; adding a Status means revisiting every row.

## Why a transition table but no generated diagram

Session state has been stable where task status has not. Twelve session-related
schema change files exist and not one touches `state`'s value set — sessions have
churned through short ids, nullable session_id, active epic, kind, gates added
and dropped, transcript path dropped, recap columns dropped, and the four values
held throughout. The live database has exactly four distinct values ever written.
Task status gained three members over a comparable stretch.

The two are different kinds of vocabulary. Task status models a human approval
workflow, which keeps acquiring distinctions people find worth drawing; session
state models a process lifecycle written by hooks, bounded by what a harness can
report. Realistic growth is one member (E-2091's fifth), plausibly a second for
stall detection.

So `taskstatus`'s generated-mermaid machinery — the artifact, the regeneration
recipe, the drift check, the three-copy sync test — is not justified here. It
earns its keep against thirteen states with per-task-type edges people
misremember. Four hook-written states do not have that problem.

The transition TABLE is justified on different grounds: its `trigger` column
names which code performs each write. "What actually writes `needs_input`?" is
the question that produced the wrong proposal above, and it stays expensive at
four states or six, because it is a question about writers scattered across two
languages rather than about how many values exist.

## Decisions taken with Mike (2026-09-01)

1. Pure refactor. No state is added here; E-2091 adds the fifth. The verification
   gate is behaviour byte-identical before and after, which is the only cheap way
   to prove a 70-site conversion broke nothing.
2. Five groups: All, Live, MayWrite, AwaitsHuman, DisplayOrder.
3. Transition table as data plus a test. No generated artifact.
4. Python converts now, not at the all-Go port. If Python keeps its own copy,
   E-2091's fifth state is rejected by `--state`'s Click choice and renders as
   the unknown glyph — the exact missed-site incident this pattern exists to
   prevent, and it would defeat the point of doing this task first.

payload.title: Refuse a resume whose Claude transcript is gone, and route the user instead
payload.description: Endless resolves a resume target out of sessions.session_id and hands the UUID to `claude --resume` without checking the transcript still exists, so a lost transcript dead-ends differently at each entry point: `session goto --resume` silently does nothing, `session resume` shows only Claude's own error, and neither names the route back (a fresh session plus `task claim`, or `task bind`). Also replace `claim`'s stale "choose one" block, whose first option `task spawn` is refused on any re-claim, with the single next step. Found trying to pick E-1934 back up after its claiming session ended in thirty seconds.
payload.analysis:
Endless resolves a resume target out of `sessions.session_id` and hands the UUID
to `claude --resume` without ever checking that the transcript still exists, so
a session whose transcript is gone fails differently at each entry point and
never routes the user anywhere. Found while trying to pick E-1934 back up: its
claiming session ended after thirty seconds and its transcript is absent from
disk and from every Time Machine backup taken after it ran.

(a) `session goto <ref> --resume` appears to do nothing. `_open_resume_window`
passes the `claude --resume` command line to `tmux new-window`, which succeeds
because the window really was created, so Endless reports `(new window)` and
returns a pane id. The claude process inside then exits on the missing
transcript and the window closes. No error reaches the caller.

(b) `session resume <ref>` reports only Claude's own error. `resume_session`
execs `claude --resume` directly, so nothing says what Endless resolved or what
to do instead. `--dry-run` against the same ref resolves cleanly and prints a
worktree, which makes the failure look unrelated to the transcript.

Both should stat the transcript before launching and refuse with a route rather
than a dead end. The route exists: a task whose claimant has ended is still
claimable, so a fresh Claude session plus `task claim` picks the work up, and
`task bind` attaches ownership without moving status. Neither is discoverable
from the failure today.

(c) `claim_item` prints a "To work on this task, choose one:" block after every
claim, and both options are wrong for the case that reaches it most often — a
re-claim onto a task whose worktree already exists. Option 1 offers
`task spawn`, which `_check_prior_claim` refuses whenever the task has any prior
claimant, which a re-claim always does. Option 2 spells out `/cd`, `shell-init`
and `eswt`. Replace the whole block with the single next step:

    To open Claude to work on this task, run:

       endless session resume E-<id>

Note for the implementer: after a claim made from a Claude pane, that resume ref
resolves to the claiming session itself. Decide whether the block should be
conditional on where the claim was run from.

Verify by claiming a task whose worktree already exists and reading the output,
and by pointing both resume paths at a session whose transcript file has been
removed.

triage.rationale: The description names the problem and desired outcomes but doesn't specify how each entry point should detect the missing transcript, what the unified error/routing message should say, or how it decides between recommending `task claim` vs `task bind`.

fields.description: tasks.description is a short single-line metadata field, so a --description-file loader (added alongside the other --xxx-file flags) has no real use — you would never load a one-line summary from a file. Two changes, one unit: drop the write-time cap from 1024 to 384 chars so a description cannot grow into a document, and remove --description-file. Coordinate with the inline-flag path gate: with the flag gone, the gate's redirect for a path mis-passed to --description can no longer say 'use --description-file' and should instead say descriptions are short inline text. The loader also never stripped a trailing newline, so any file written by echo, a heredoc or an editor tripped the one-line rule and had to be re-emitted with printf; removing the flag removes that trap with it.

triage.rationale: The description fully specifies both changes (drop cap to 384 chars, remove --description-file flag) plus the exact updated gate message and rationale, leaving no material decision to an implementer.

payload.title: Distinguish a never-started task from a started-and-settled one in session status
payload.description: The one column between the task-type letter and the id in session status (unsettledMark) has two states: diamond for unsettled, blank otherwise. The blank collapses 'nobody has started this' and 'work is done and in, nothing left to land' — opposite next moves, identical rendering. Add a third state meaning underway-but-not-unsettled, so blank comes to mean exactly one thing: never started.
payload.analysis:
`session status` renders one column between the task-type letter and the task
id (`unsettledMark`, internal/sessionstatuscmd/session_status.go). It has two
states today: ◆ when the row's worktree is unsettled, and a blank otherwise.

The blank collapses states that mean opposite things to a reader:

- A task nobody has started. There is no worktree, nothing has been written,
  and the next move is to claim it.
- A task whose work is done and in — non-terminal status, worktree settled,
  nothing left to land. The next move is to verify or close it.

Both render identically, so the flat view cannot answer "has anything happened
here yet?" — which is the question being asked when scanning it.

Add a third state to that column: a glyph meaning **underway but not
unsettled**, i.e. work has begun and nothing is currently outstanding. Blank
then means exactly one thing — never started — which is the distinction being
asked for.

The signal to key on is already computed and needs no new probe:
`monitor.UnsettledDetail.HasWorktree` (worktree_unsettled.go). A task with a
worktree that is settled has been started; a task with no worktree has not.
`SessionStatusRow` carries `Unsettled` today and would need the second flag
alongside it, filled by the same `AnnotateSessionStatusUnsettled` pass.

Constraints the existing column imposes:

- The glyph must be display width 1. The prefix is a fixed 13 columns and the
  alignment guarantee ⏚/⁇/◆ carry (E-1765) holds only if every state in this
  slot is the same width.
- It must not clash with the glyphs already in play: ● ↩ ✓ ◆ ⊗ ⏸ ⊘ ⊕ · ⏚ ⁇,
  nor with --tree's leading focal marker.
- `buildLegend` shows a decoration only when a row bears it; the new glyph
  follows that rule and is labelled there.
- ◆ vetoes dimming (E-1707) because it means "still something to do". The new
  glyph means the opposite, so it must NOT veto dimming — a settled, done row
  should still be able to read as done.

fields.description: Endless never wired Claude Code's `Notification` hook, so nothing observes a permission prompt: a session sitting on one reads as `working`, indistinguishable from one doing work. E-1976 built the display side and left the producer out — its board's first rank (⚠ waiting) has none. Install the hook, add a `prompted` state to internal/sessionstate and classify it into all five groups (MayWrite included, so approving a prompt never leaves the session refused), route `permission_prompt` to it and `idle_prompt` to `idle`, clear it on the session's next activity, and admit it to the board. Deliberately NOT reusing `needs_input`: the declaration gate enforces the opposite meaning on that state. Blocked by E-2105, which gives the vocabulary an owning package.
fields.text:
# Plan — make the board's ⚠ rank real

Blocked by E-2105, which gives the session state vocabulary an owning package.
Every step below assumes `internal/sessionstate` exists and that Python reads the
vocabulary from it rather than holding a copy.

## 1. Install the hook

Add `Notification` to `CLAUDE_HOOK_EVENTS` in `src/endless/setup.py`.

NOT in `SYNC_EVENTS`. The handler records a state and gates nothing, so it has no
reason to block the harness; every event in that set is there because something
downstream reads what it wrote within the same turn.

Existing installs matter more than fresh ones here. `setup.py` already re-writes
hook entries whose configuration has drifted — the mechanism E-1911 added so a
machine running a stale async `Stop` would not keep reporting itself correctly
set up. Confirm that detection reports an event that is MISSING ENTIRELY, not
only one whose entry is mis-shaped; if it only inspects entries that exist,
extend it. Without that, every machine already running Endless keeps six hooks
and never gains the seventh, while `setup` reports success.

## 2. The state

Add `Prompted` to `internal/sessionstate`, and classify it into all five groups —
which the package makes unskippable:

| Group          | Member? | Why |
|----------------|---------|-----|
| `All`          | yes     | `working, prompted, idle, needs_input, ended` — lifecycle order, `prompted` beside `working` because it is a mid-turn state |
| `Live`         | yes     | the session is running |
| `MayWrite`     | **yes** | decided 2026-09-01; see the analysis |
| `AwaitsHuman`  | yes     | it is the definition of the group |
| `DisplayOrder` | first   | `prompted, working, needs_input, idle, ended` — `session list` sorts loudest first, and nothing claims attention harder |

Label `prompted`. Glyph `⚠`, the glyph E-1976's board already uses for the rank;
it measures one column under `go-runewidth`, which the vocabulary's glyph test
asserts for every member.

Transition rows: `any → prompted` (Notification / `monitor.PromptSession`) and
`prompted → working` (see §4).

## 3. The handler

`case "Notification":` in `internal/hookcmd/claude.go`, reading the notification
kind from the payload and acting on exactly two values:

- `permission_prompt` → `monitor.PromptSession(sessionID)`, a new helper beside
  `IdleSession`/`EndSession` writing `state='prompted'` and refreshing
  `last_activity`.
- `idle_prompt` → `monitor.IdleSession(sessionID)`. It means the input prompt sat
  untouched for 60 seconds, which is what `idle` already says; giving it its own
  state would split one meaning across two.

move the session, and an unrecognised kind is the shape a harness change arrives
in. The payload's field name for the kind is read off the hook's JSON at
implementation — a lookup, not a choice.

`monitor.ParseTranscript` is NOT called here. Notification is not a turn
boundary and carries no new messages.

`prompted` returns to `working` on the session's next activity, via a
`monitor.ResumeFromPrompt(sessionID)` that updates only when the current state is

`UserPromptSubmit` (the user typed instead). `Stop` needs no change — it writes
`idle` unconditionally, which is correct for a turn that ended while a prompt was
outstanding.

Deliberately NOT folded into `TouchSession`: that helper never clobbers a live
state, and making it the exception for one value is how a general helper starts
carrying special cases.

next Stop. It cannot refuse anyone.

analysis gives — 34 dead placeholder rows would flood the rank this task exists

producer", it is "the placeholder is not this rank".

   `internal/monitor`, `internal/projectstatuscmd`, and the Python suite.
2. `Prompted` is in `MayWrite` — asserted directly, because it is the decision
   the whole design turns on and its absence is a wedged session, not a wrong
   glyph.
3. The declaration gate admits a `prompted` session: drive `sessionMayWrite`

fields.analysis:
## What is missing

Endless installs six Claude Code hooks — PreToolUse, SessionStart,
UserPromptSubmit, PostToolUse, Stop, SessionEnd. None fires when Claude Code asks
the user for permission, so a session sitting on a prompt is indistinguishable
from one doing work: both read `working`, with a last_activity that stopped
moving. `Notification` is the event that reports it, and it was never wired.

E-1976 built the display side and left the producer out. `actWaiting` is the
board's first rank, wears ⚠, renders bold, and `classify()` already routes a
state to it. The rank has no producer, which is this task.

## Why a new state rather than `needs_input`

`needs_input` looks like the obvious home and is not. It is ENFORCED:
`hookcmd.sessionMayWrite` refuses file writes from a session in that state under
`enforce` tracking, with the message "you asked your user something and the
answer has not arrived. There is no command for you to run."

That state means the AGENT asked the USER something. A permission prompt is the
reverse — the agent is trying to act and the harness is asking — and routing one
to the other would refuse the session's next write after the user approved.

The near miss is worth recording because it was not carelessness. The gate's
admission set was a Go `switch` with a silent `default: return false`, so a new
state joined the refused set without anyone deciding it should. That is why
E-2105 came first: with `MayWrite` a named group, adding a state cannot skip the
question.

## Why `prompted` may write

Decided with Mike (2026-09-01), from the gate's own stated rule rather than from
preference. The gate admits a session that "has DECLARED what it is working on
and is live-and-acting", and it already glosses `idle` as admissible because "a
write from an idle session is by definition mid-turn". A prompt-blocked session
is mid-turn by exactly that reasoning, and the tool it waits on is its own.

The decisive argument was the asymmetry of failure modes. Both readings need a
clearing transition. If the clear misses under this one, a stale ⚠ sits on the
board until the next Stop — cosmetic, self-correcting. If it missed under the
other, every prompted session would be refused its next write and told there is
no command to run, which is the failure E-2093 was cleaning up after.

It also makes the design robust to something not verifiable from the code: it
does not matter whether PostToolUse fires when permission is DENIED.

## What this is for

E-1815's auto-spawn must not proceed past a pending permission prompt. A prompt
is a claim on the user's attention, and the spawn governor's premise is that it
measures such claims — a premise that cannot hold while the claim is invisible.
Until this lands, the board ranks `idle`/`working` and the governor is reasoning
about something it cannot see.

## A residue this deliberately does not clean up

`needs_input` remains written only by INSERT (`monitor.InitSession`) and by the
revive-an-ended-row CASE. Measured while E-1976 was built: 34 rows in `endless`
carrying it, every one last active 25 to 71 days earlier, none on a pane that
still existed. They are sessions that registered and never had a turn.

So the board keeps excluding `needs_input` after this task, for the reason it
already excludes it. Widening the board to all of `Live` would let that sediment
flood the very rank this task exists to make trustworthy. Making `needs_input`
mean what its name says — by writing `idle` on INSERT and retiring the existing
rows — is a separate change with its own migration, and folding it in here would
mix a data cleanup into an enforcement-adjacent feature.

## What the column says today

`session status` renders one column between the task-type letter and the task
id (`unsettledMark`, internal/sessionstatuscmd/session_status.go). Two states:
◆ when the row's worktree is unsettled, blank otherwise.

## What is being asked for

The column should answer "is there work product here, and where is it?" —
three states, not two:

| State | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| ◆ | work product, still outstanding | anything unsettled |
| *new glyph* | **no work product yet** | never spawned (no worktree) **or** `underway` with a settled worktree |
| blank | work product, all of it landed | `unverified` + settled |

The two cases sharing the new glyph are deliberate and are the point of the
task: a task nobody has picked up and a task a session is sitting on that has
produced nothing are the same fact about the work. The reader does not need
the glyph to tell those apart — the status and session columns already do —
so the glyph must not try to.

That is the correction to the first framing of this task, which had the new
glyph marking `underway`-and-settled ALONE and left never-spawned blank. That
splits the two states that mean the same thing and merges the two that do not.

## The one design choice

What distinguishes "underway + settled" (glyph) from "unverified + settled"
(blank)? Both have a clean worktree with nothing outstanding.

**Option A — read the status.** `underway` means nothing produced yet;
`unverified`/terminal means produced and in. Cheap, needs no new probe, uses
data already on `SessionStatusRow`, and reproduces every case named above. Its
mis-signal: a task that landed mid-flight and kept working is `underway` with
real landed work, and would wear the glyph. That reads as "nothing here yet"
when there is something — but it is also true that there is nothing
outstanding, so the mis-signal is mild.

**Option B — ask whether anything ever landed.** Truer to the words, but
`task_landings` is not a reliable record of it: E-2087 measured branches whose
work is demonstrably on main with no landing row at all (E-1834, E-1934). A
git-side answer exists — `git log <base> --grep "E-<id>:"`, since the guide
mandates that commit-subject form — but it is a new probe on the hot path.

Recommend A, and say in the legend what the glyph means rather than what it is
derived from, so B can replace it later without the vocabulary changing.

  guarantee ⏚/⁇/◆ carry (E-1765) holds only if every state in the slot
  matches.
- No clash with ● ↩ ✓ ◆ ⊗ ⏸ ⊘ ⊕ · ⏚ ⁇, nor with --tree's leading focal marker.
- `buildLegend` shows a decoration only when a row bears it; the new glyph
  follows that rule and is labelled there.
- ◆ vetoes dimming (E-1707) because it means "still something to do". The new
  glyph means the opposite and must NOT veto dimming — a never-started `later`
  row should still read dim.

Endless resolves a resume target out of `sessions.session_id` and hands the UUID
to `claude --resume` without ever checking that the transcript still exists, so
a session whose transcript is gone fails differently at each entry point and
never routes the user anywhere. Found while trying to pick E-1934 back up: its
claiming session ended after thirty seconds and its transcript is absent from
disk and from every Time Machine backup taken after it ran.

(a) `session goto <ref> --resume` appears to do nothing. `_open_resume_window`
passes the `claude --resume` command line to `tmux new-window`, which succeeds
because the window really was created, so Endless reports `(new window)` and
returns a pane id. The claude process inside then exits on the missing
transcript and the window closes. No error reaches the caller.

(b) `session resume <ref>` reports only Claude's own error. `resume_session`
execs `claude --resume` directly, so nothing says what Endless resolved or what
to do instead. `--dry-run` against the same ref resolves cleanly and prints a
worktree, which makes the failure look unrelated to the transcript.

Both should stat the transcript before launching and refuse with a route rather
than a dead end. The route exists: a task whose claimant has ended is still
claimable, so a fresh Claude session plus `task claim` picks the work up, and
`task bind` attaches ownership without moving status. Neither is discoverable
from the failure today.

(c) `claim_item` prints a "To work on this task, choose one:" block after every
claim, and both options are wrong for the case that reaches it most often — a
re-claim onto a task whose worktree already exists. Option 1 offers
`task spawn`, which `_check_prior_claim` refuses whenever the task has any prior
claimant, which a re-claim always does. Option 2 spells out `/cd`, `shell-init`
and `eswt`.

## What claim should print instead, by caller

Replace the block with one outcome per caller, decided from how the bound
session resolved. `_resolve_session_id_with_prompt` returns a bare id today and
does not report which layer produced it, so it needs to report provenance —
env/pane, sibling pane, or nothing — before this can branch.

1. Claim ran INSIDE the Claude session being bound (env or direct pane match).
   Print `/cd <worktree>` and nothing else. The session is already here; it only
   needs its working directory moved. Mike would almost never claim this way,
   but another user might, and it should work rather than fail.

2. Claim ran from a shell, no tmux. Refuse: tmux is required.

3. Claim ran from a shell inside a tmux window holding one pane. Do the work:
   split the window into two siblings — horizontal running `esm`
   (`endless session monitor`), vertical running nothing.
   (Mike wrote "windows"; horizontal/vertical splits are panes, so panes is the
   reading taken here. Confirm before implementing if that is wrong.)

4. Claim resolved a Claude session in a SIBLING pane. Refuse and say to run
   `session goto --resume` instead. Deliberately not handled: covering it means
   deciding what happens to every other pane and window in play, and tmux panes
   are cheap enough that the complexity is not worth the benefit.

5. `--unattended`. Note for whoever picks this up: it is NOT the background-task
   flag and not an auto-spawn flag — background sessions were removed by E-2074.
   E-2093 split `claim --force`, which used to spell two unrelated decisions, and
   `--unattended` is the half that means "claim with NO Claude session bound":
   manual work at a terminal, a plain shell, cron. So there is no Claude session
   to route to and no resume to offer. Print the worktree and stop.

Verify by claiming a task whose worktree already exists from each of the five
callers above, and by pointing both resume paths at a session whose transcript
file has been removed.

Settled design, from working through it with Mike. Part 2 of the original
description is already done: ED-1073 was widened the same morning E-1934 was
filed and now reads "no time-frozen specifics in any durable field", enumerating
description, analysis, text/plan, outcome and decision bodies. What remains is
the gate (part 1) and the guide wording (part 3).

## Rule 3 — line citations

`_guard_inline_content` has Rule 1 (whole value is a path token) and Rule 2 (an
absolute path token anywhere). Rule 3 refuses a line citation.

- Matches `<name>.<ext>:<digits>` where `<ext>` is in the citation-extension
  set. Also `<name>.<ext>:<digits>-<digits>` (range) and
  `<name>.<ext>:<digits>:<digits>` (line:col).
- Does NOT match a bare leading-colon number. Nobody writes a bare line number
  that way, and the false positives are everywhere: clock times, host:port,
  ratios.
- Skips any token preceded by a scheme separator or an at-sign, or beginning
  with a www prefix. This is what keeps host:port out of the gate, and it is
  load-bearing rather than belt-and-braces: many source extensions ARE ccTLDs
  (Serbia, Paraguay, Poland, Saint Helena, Mali, Cocos, Moldova), so the
  extension set alone does not separate a file citation from a domain.
- No escape hatch. Rule 2 has one; Rule 3 does not.
- Applies wherever Rule 2 applies: description, text/plan, analysis, outcome and
  decision bodies. E-1992 collapses these into task_content, at which point the
  gate stops enumerating flags and guards content.

## Configuration

Three keys under a content block in the project config file, which already
carries list-valued keys, so no new shape is needed.

- A built-in default extension set of roughly eighty entries covering systems,
  JVM and .NET, scripting, JS/TS and web, functional, data and config, docs,
  and build and schema files.
- Two thin override lists layered over that default rather than replacing it,
  so a project adding or removing one extension does not restate eighty.
  OPEN: the allow/deny naming inverts depending on the reader's model — "allow"
  can mean "add this extension to what the gate matches" or "permit this
  extension in content", which are opposites. Settle the names before building.

  trouble than it is worth. Worth giving Rule 2 its own switch at the same time,

`_builtin_allowed_dirs` exempts endless's own config and cache directories, and
its docstring already anticipates being extended at that composition point.

that absolute paths are non-portable and that a temp path dies with the
worktree; neither is true of a tool's conventional dot-directory under home,
which names the same location for every user on every machine. Home-relative
paths that are NOT dot-directories stay refused — a personal projects directory
really is machine-specific. Encountered live: writing a lesson about the Claude
transcript directory was refused, and the text had to be degraded to prose that
named no location.

The tasks guide still describes text as a full implementation plan "including
approach, file paths, verification steps", which invites the thing ED-1073

file and function names.

2. Claim ran from a shell, no tmux. Refuse: tmux is required.

3. Claim ran from a shell inside a tmux window holding one pane. Do the work:
   split the window into two sibling PANES — horizontal running `esm`
   (`endless session monitor`), vertical running nothing. Confirmed by Mike.

4. Claim resolved a Claude session in a SIBLING pane. Refuse and say to run
   `session goto --resume` instead. Deliberately not handled: covering it means
   deciding what happens to every other pane and window in play, and tmux panes
   are cheap enough that the complexity is not worth the benefit.

5. `--unattended`. E-2093 split `claim --force`, which used to spell two
   unrelated decisions; this is the half meaning "claim with NO Claude session
   bound". Without it, a claim from a plain shell with no Claude anywhere is
   refused. With it, the task is claimed and `sessions.task_id` is left unset.
   So there is no session to route to and no resume to offer: print the worktree
   and stop.

   The NAME is wrong and Mike flagged it. "Unattended" describes automation
   running unsupervised, but the flag's primary use is a HUMAN working by hand
   at a terminal — very much attended. What is absent is a bound Claude session,
   not a person. It is also one letter of intent away from the global
   `--no-session`, which governs event ATTRIBUTION rather than binding, and
   claim's own docstring already spends a paragraph warning the two apart.
   Rename it to name what is absent — `--unbound` or `--no-bind`. Out of scope
   here; file separately if wanted.

Verify by claiming a task whose worktree already exists from each of the five
callers above, and by pointing both resume paths at a session whose transcript
file has been removed.

Settled design, from working through it with Mike. Part 2 of the original
description is already done: ED-1073 was widened the same morning E-1934 was
filed and now reads "no time-frozen specifics in any durable field", enumerating
description, analysis, text/plan, outcome and decision bodies. What remains is
the gate (part 1) and the guide wording (part 3).

## Rule 3 — line citations

`_guard_inline_content` has Rule 1 (whole value is a path token) and Rule 2 (an
absolute path token anywhere). Rule 3 refuses a line citation.

- Matches `<name>.<ext>:<digits>` where `<ext>` is in the citation-extension
  set. Also `<name>.<ext>:<digits>-<digits>` (range) and
  `<name>.<ext>:<digits>:<digits>` (line:col).
- Does NOT match a bare leading-colon number. Nobody writes a bare line number
  that way, and the false positives are everywhere: clock times, host:port,
  ratios.
- Skips any token preceded by a scheme separator or an at-sign, or beginning
  with a www prefix. This is what keeps host:port out of the gate, and it is
  load-bearing rather than belt-and-braces: many source extensions ARE ccTLDs
  (Serbia, Paraguay, Poland, Saint Helena, Mali, Cocos, Moldova), so the
  extension set alone does not separate a file citation from a domain.
- No escape hatch. Rule 2 has one; Rule 3 does not.
- Applies wherever Rule 2 applies: description, text/plan, analysis, outcome and
  decision bodies. E-1992 collapses these into task_content, at which point the
  gate stops enumerating flags and guards content.

## Configuration

Three keys under a content block in the project config file, which already
carries list-valued keys, so no new shape is needed.

- A built-in default extension set of roughly eighty entries covering systems,
  JVM and .NET, scripting, JS/TS and web, functional, data and config, docs,
  and build and schema files.
- Two thin override lists layered over that default rather than replacing it,
  so a project adding or removing one extension does not restate eighty. Named
  `content.extensions.block` and `content.extensions.unblock`, nested. The verb
  attaches to the behaviour rather than to set membership, which is what makes
  it readable a year later: block names one more extension whose citations are
  refused, unblock stops refusing one the default covers. Earlier candidates
  spelled around an abstract "set the gate matches" and every one of them was
  ambiguous in one direction or the other.
- An extension listed in BOTH lists is a config error and must be refused at
  load, not silently resolved. That follows the house pattern already set by
  --clear against a field flag, and by --status against --keep-status: when two
  settings spell contradictory intent, refuse and say so.
- A switch that disables the gate outright, for a project that finds it more
  trouble than it is worth, nested alongside as `content.extensions` sits under
  `content`. Worth giving Rule 2 its own switch at the same time, by the same
  reasoning.

## Widening the built-in path exemption

`_builtin_allowed_dirs` exempts endless's own config and cache directories, and
its docstring already anticipates being extended at that composition point.
Widen it to any dot-directory directly under home. Rule 2's stated rationale is
that absolute paths are non-portable and that a temp path dies with the
worktree; neither is true of a tool's conventional dot-directory under home,
which names the same location for every user on every machine. Home-relative
paths that are NOT dot-directories stay refused — a personal projects directory
really is machine-specific. Encountered live: writing a lesson about the Claude
transcript directory was refused, and the text had to be degraded to prose that
named no location.

## Part 3 — guide wording

The tasks guide still describes text as a full implementation plan "including
approach, file paths, verification steps", which invites the thing ED-1073
forbids, and says nothing about line numbers anywhere. Fix the wording to say
file and function names.

fields.title: Wire the Notification hook and record when a session is waiting on the user
fields.description: Endless never wired Claude Code's Notification hook, so it cannot see a session paused on a permission prompt — that session reads 'working', indistinguishable from one doing work. E-1976 built the display side and left the producer out: its board's first rank has none. Install the hook, add a 'prompted' state to internal/sessionstate classified into all five groups (MayWrite included, so approving a prompt never leaves the session refused), route notification_type permission_prompt to it and idle_prompt to idle, and clear it on the session's next activity. Waiting on the user means the session paused for input, question or not, so AwaitsHuman becomes the one place that answers it. Also stops InitSession and the revive CASE from writing needs_input, and reveals those rows on the board instead of hiding them.
fields.text:
# Plan — record when a session is waiting on the user

Blocked by E-2105, which gives the session state vocabulary an owning package.
Every step assumes `internal/sessionstate` exists and that Python reads the
vocabulary from it rather than holding a copy.

## 1. Install the hook

Add `Notification` to `CLAUDE_HOOK_EVENTS` in `src/endless/setup.py`.

NOT in `SYNC_EVENTS`: the handler records a state and gates nothing, so it has no
reason to block the harness. Every member of that set is there because something
downstream reads what it wrote within the same turn.

Existing installs need nothing extra. `_repair_missing_hook_events` already adds
an endless-go entry for any hooked event that has none, precisely so a machine
whose install predates an event still gains it — verified, not assumed.

## 2. The state

Add `Prompted` to `internal/sessionstate` and classify it into all five groups,
which the package makes unskippable:

| Group          | Member? | Why |
|----------------|---------|-----|
| `All`          | yes     | `working, prompted, idle, needs_input, ended` — lifecycle order; beside `working` because it is a mid-turn state |
| `Live`         | yes     | the session is running |
| `MayWrite`     | **yes** | decided 2026-09-01; see the analysis |
| `AwaitsHuman`  | yes     | it is the definition of the group |
| `DisplayOrder` | first   | `prompted, working, needs_input, idle, ended` |

Label `prompted`. Glyph the warning sign E-1976's board already uses for the
rank; it measures one column under go-runewidth, which the vocabulary's glyph
test asserts for every member.

Transition rows: `any -> prompted` (Notification / `monitor.PromptSession`) and
`prompted -> working` (see §4).

`AwaitsHuman` is the group that carries this task's definition of waiting: after
this change it holds `idle`, `needs_input` and `prompted` — every state in which
the session has paused for the user, question or no question. Anything that needs
to ask "is this session waiting on me" asks that group, not a list of states.

## 3. The handler

`case "Notification":` in `internal/hookcmd/claude.go`, reading the payload's
`notification_type` field and acting on exactly two values:

- `permission_prompt` -> `monitor.PromptSession(sessionID)`, a new helper beside
  `IdleSession`/`EndSession` writing the `prompted` state and refreshing
  `last_activity`.
- `idle_prompt` -> `monitor.IdleSession(sessionID)`. It means the input prompt
  sat untouched for 60 seconds, which is what `idle` already says. Idempotent on
  a session already idle.

Every other value writes no state. `notification_type` carries at least a dozen
documented values — auth, elicitation, quota, agent-team — and a notification
Endless does not model must not move the session. An unrecognised value is also
the shape a harness change arrives in.

`claudePayload` gains `NotificationType string` with the `notification_type` tag.

`monitor.ParseTranscript` is NOT called here: Notification is not a turn boundary
and carries no new messages.

## 4. Clearing it

`prompted` returns to `working` on the session's next activity, via
`monitor.ResumeFromPrompt(sessionID)` which updates only when the current state
is `prompted`, so it can never demote a session that moved on another way.

Called from `PostToolUse` (the approved tool completed) and `UserPromptSubmit`
(the user typed instead). `Stop` needs no change: it writes `idle`
unconditionally, correct for a turn that ended with a prompt outstanding.

Deliberately NOT folded into `TouchSession`, which never clobbers a live state;
making it the exception for one value is how a general helper starts carrying
special cases.

Because `prompted` is in `MayWrite`, a missed clear costs a stale glyph until the
next Stop. It cannot refuse anyone.

## 5. Stop making new `needs_input` sediment

`monitor.InitSession` writes `needs_input` as a row's initial value, and the
revive-an-ended-row CASE (`monitor.TouchSession`, `internal/events/executor.go`)
writes it on any incoming hook. Neither means a person is being waited on.

Both become `idle`, which is what they actually mean: the session exists and is
not doing anything. `needs_input` is then written by nothing, and means only what
the declaration gate says.

The 34 existing rows are NOT migrated. They are surfaced by §6 so they can be
resolved deliberately; retiring them automatically is the opposite of what
revealing them is for.

## 6. Reveal them on the board

`internal/monitor/project_status.go`: `boardSessionStates` is deleted, and the
session query filters on `sessionstate.SQLList(sessionstate.Live)`. E-1976's
exclusion of `needs_input` goes with it, along with its comment.

`internal/projectstatuscmd/board.go`: `classify()` routes `prompted` to
`actWaiting`, alongside the existing `needs_input` arm. Both are waiting on the
user; the board's age column already distinguishes a live prompt from a
two-month-old row on sight, which is what that column is for.

## 7. What this does NOT change

The board's RANK ORDER. `idle` sits sixth of seven today, which under this
task's definition of waiting is arguably too low — but that is a display
question, and the board's UI is being reshaped separately. Recognising state and
displaying it are orthogonal; this task does the first, completely, and leaves
the second alone so the redesign is not pre-empted.

No classification of how a turn ended, no reading of the final assistant message,
and no dependency on the minimizer, which is disabled and out of this task's
critical path by decision.

## 8. Python

None, if E-2105 landed as planned: the `--state` choice and the glyph map both
come from the registry, so `prompted` flows through. Verify rather than assume —
`endless session list --state prompted` must be accepted and must render the
warning glyph.

## 9. Migration

None. No row carries `prompted` today and no existing value changes meaning.

## 10. Verification

`.endless/tasks/e-2091/verify.sh`, sourcing `_harness.sh`:

1. Fail-fast unit gate: `internal/sessionstate`, `internal/hookcmd`,
   `internal/monitor`, `internal/projectstatuscmd`, and the Python suite.
2. `Prompted` is in `MayWrite` — asserted directly, because it is the decision
   the design turns on and its absence is a wedged session, not a wrong glyph.
3. The declaration gate admits a prompted session: drive `sessionMayWrite` with
   a prompted session holding a task and assert it may write.
4. `AwaitsHuman` holds `idle`, `needs_input` and `prompted` — the vocabulary's
   statement of what waiting means, pinned so a later edit is deliberate.
5. State machine round trip: `PromptSession` then `ResumeFromPrompt` yields
   `working`; `ResumeFromPrompt` on a working session is a no-op; `Stop` from
   `prompted` yields `idle`.
6. The handler routes `permission_prompt` and `idle_prompt` and IGNORES a third
   value, asserted against synthetic payloads rather than a live harness.
7. No writer produces `needs_input`: a sweep asserting `InitSession` and the
   revive CASE write `idle`, plus a seeded SessionStart landing on `idle`.
8. `setup.py` installs seven events with `Notification` among them and not in
   `SYNC_EVENTS`, and a settings file carrying only the old six is repaired to
   seven rather than reported correct.
9. End to end against a seeded throwaway database: a prompted session renders as
   the board's first row, and a `needs_input` session renders rather than being
   suppressed.
fields.analysis:
## What is missing

Endless installs six Claude Code hooks — PreToolUse, SessionStart,
UserPromptSubmit, PostToolUse, Stop, SessionEnd. None reports that Claude Code is
asking the user for permission, so a session sitting on a prompt reads `working`,
indistinguishable from one doing work. `Notification` is the event that reports
it and was never wired.

E-1976 built the display side and left the producer out: `actWaiting` is the
board's first rank, wears the warning glyph, renders bold, and `classify()`
already routes a state to it. The rank has no producer. That is this task.

## What "waiting on the user" means here

Decided with Mike (2026-09-03): a session is waiting on the user whenever it has
paused for input, whether or not it asked a question. A finished turn and a
question are the same thing for this purpose — the ball is in the user's court —
which is exactly what his tmux window flag already signals and has proven
accurate in practice.

That definition is what keeps the task small. There is no question-versus-
finished classification, no inspection of the turn's final message, and no model
call. `idle` already means "the turn ended", so the work is to add the one
paused-for-input case Endless cannot currently see — a permission prompt — and to
make the vocabulary say that both are the same kind of waiting.

Explicitly not coupled to the minimizer. It is disabled until further notice,
will be renamed when it returns, and nothing on this task's critical path may
depend on it.

## What the current hooks reference says

Checked against the live documentation rather than recall, which was two months
and twenty-four events out of date.

Claude Code exposes 33 hook events. `Notification` carries a `notification_type`
field whose documented values include `permission_prompt` and `idle_prompt`.

Two findings that shaped the design:

- `agent_needs_input` exists but is scoped to agent-team teammates about to go
  idle, alongside a `TeammateIdle` event. It is NOT a main-session "the agent
  asked you something" signal, and designing on it would have been wrong.
- `PermissionRequest` is now a first-class event carrying `tool_name`,
  `tool_input` and `tool_use_id`. It is nevertheless the wrong signal for this
  task: it fires whenever a permission DECISION is needed, which an allowlist or
  another hook can resolve without the user ever seeing anything.
  `Notification` with `permission_prompt` fires when the user is actually
  prompted, which is the fact this task records.

## Why a new state rather than `needs_input`

`needs_input` looks like the obvious home and is not. It is ENFORCED:
`hookcmd.sessionMayWrite` refuses file writes from a session in that state under
`enforce` tracking, with the message "you asked your user something and the
answer has not arrived. There is no command for you to run."

That state means the AGENT asked the USER something. A permission prompt is the
reverse — the agent is trying to act and the harness is asking — and routing one
to the other would refuse the session's next write after the user approved.

The near miss is worth recording because it was not carelessness. The gate's
admission set was a Go `switch` with a silent `default: return false`, so a new
state joined the refused set without anyone deciding it should. That is why
E-2105 came first: with `MayWrite` a named group, a state cannot be added
without the question being answered.

## Why `prompted` may write

Decided with Mike (2026-09-01), from the gate's own stated rule rather than from
preference. The gate admits a session that "has DECLARED what it is working on
and is live-and-acting", and already glosses `idle` as admissible because "a
write from an idle session is by definition mid-turn". A prompt-blocked session
is mid-turn by exactly that reasoning, and the tool it waits on is its own.

The decisive argument was the asymmetry of failure modes. Both readings need a
clearing transition. If the clear misses under this one, a stale glyph sits on
the board until the next Stop — cosmetic, self-correcting. If it missed under the
other, every prompted session would be refused its next write and told there is
no command to run, which is the failure E-2093 was cleaning up after.

## The `needs_input` writers are the real defect underneath

Two writers put `needs_input` in the database and neither means a person is being
waited on: `monitor.InitSession` writes it as a row's initial value at
SessionStart, and the revive-an-ended-row CASE writes it on any incoming hook
(E-1686). Nothing else writes it.

Measured while E-1976 was built: 34 rows in `endless` carrying it, every one last
active 25 to 71 days earlier, none on a pane that still existed — sessions that
registered and never had a turn.

E-1976 responded by excluding the state from the board. Mike's correction
(2026-09-03): that is backwards. Hiding them is how they rotted unseen, the board
already caps each rank at ten rows with a footer naming the remainder — machinery
built for exactly this — and revealing them is what provides the mechanism to
resolve them.

So this task reveals the rows and fixes the writers, and deliberately does not
retire the existing 34. They are surfaced to be dealt with, not migrated away in
the dark. Once drained, `needs_input` has no writer and no rows, and means only
what the declaration gate says it means.

payload.title: Explore what an Endless session is without Claude and without tmux
payload.description: Endless assumes Claude and tmux so foundationally that the agent-less path is barely designed: claim --unattended claims a task and leaves sessions.task_id unset, so the work has no session record and no route back. If a session record is the spine, then what is absent in that case is an AGENT, not a session — which argues the flag should be --no-agent and should still mint a session, and raises the question of what a non-Claude session row holds and how it starts and ends. Map what breaks without tmux (goto, resume, monitor, status line) and without Claude (transcripts, hooks, handoff, spawn) before changing anything. Expect a follow-up research task. The --unattended rename rides along rather than landing first, since renaming a flag before deciding whether the concept survives is churn.

triage.rationale: The description explicitly frames this as exploratory mapping work with an expected follow-up research task, leaving the session schema, flag rename, and start/end semantics for non-Claude/non-tmux sessions undecided.

fields.analysis:
Endless resolves a resume target out of `sessions.session_id` and hands the UUID
to `claude --resume` without ever checking that the transcript still exists, so
a session whose transcript is gone fails differently at each entry point and
never routes the user anywhere. Found while trying to pick E-1934 back up: its
claiming session ended after thirty seconds and its transcript is absent from
disk and from every Time Machine backup taken after it ran.

(a) `session goto <ref> --resume` appears to do nothing. `_open_resume_window`
passes the `claude --resume` command line to `tmux new-window`, which succeeds
because the window really was created, so Endless reports `(new window)` and
returns a pane id. The claude process inside then exits on the missing
transcript and the window closes. No error reaches the caller.

(b) `session resume <ref>` reports only Claude's own error. `resume_session`
execs `claude --resume` directly, so nothing says what Endless resolved or what
to do instead. `--dry-run` against the same ref resolves cleanly and prints a
worktree, which makes the failure look unrelated to the transcript.

Both should stat the transcript before launching and refuse with a route rather
than a dead end. The route exists: a task whose claimant has ended is still
claimable, so a fresh Claude session plus `task claim` picks the work up, and
`task bind` attaches ownership without moving status. Neither is discoverable
from the failure today.

(c) `claim_item` prints a "To work on this task, choose one:" block after every
claim, and both options are wrong for the case that reaches it most often — a
re-claim onto a task whose worktree already exists. Option 1 offers
`task spawn`, which `_check_prior_claim` refuses whenever the task has any prior
claimant, which a re-claim always does. Option 2 spells out `/cd`, `shell-init`
and `eswt`.

## What claim should print instead, by caller

Replace the block with one outcome per caller, decided from how the bound
session resolved. `_resolve_session_id_with_prompt` returns a bare id today and
does not report which layer produced it, so it needs to report provenance —
env/pane, sibling pane, or nothing — before this can branch.

1. Claim ran INSIDE the Claude session being bound (env or direct pane match).
   Print `/cd <worktree>` and nothing else. The session is already here; it only
   needs its working directory moved. Mike would almost never claim this way,
   but another user might, and it should work rather than fail.

2. Claim ran from a shell, no tmux. Refuse: tmux is required.

3. Claim ran from a shell inside a tmux window holding one pane. Do the work:
   split the window into two sibling PANES — horizontal running `esm`
   (`endless session monitor`), vertical running nothing. Confirmed by Mike.

4. Claim resolved a Claude session in a SIBLING pane. Refuse and say to run
   `session goto --resume` instead. Deliberately not handled: covering it means
   deciding what happens to every other pane and window in play, and tmux panes
   are cheap enough that the complexity is not worth the benefit.

5. `--unattended`. Scope here is only the printed line: there is no bound
   Claude session, so there is nothing to resume. Print the worktree and stop.
   Everything else about this flag — whether an agent-less claim should mint a
   session record at all, and whether the flag should be renamed --no-agent —
   is E-2110, deliberately out of scope for this task.

Verify by claiming a task whose worktree already exists from each of the five
callers above, and by pointing both resume paths at a session whose transcript
file has been removed.

payload.title: Decide how to get the exact unlanded answer without paying for it on every tool call
payload.description: E-2087 made 'does this branch hold work the base lacks?' exact via git range-diff, then had to be reverted on the worktree reaper because the reaper runs on PreToolUse/PostToolUse and a ~90s sweep stopped the product. The display surfaces keep the exact answer; the reaper is back to the cheap SHA check and its known leak. Decide how to have both — caching keyed on branch/base tip OIDs, taking the reaper off the hook path, a cheaper exact algorithm, or fixing the landing-recording gap underneath.
payload.analysis:
## The problem

"Does this branch hold work the base branch lacks?" has an exact answer and a
cheap answer, and they are not the same answer.

- **Exact** (E-2087, `unlandedCommits` in internal/monitor/worktree_unlanded.go):
  `git range-diff` between the branch and the base since their merge base.
  Recognises a commit a rebasing land re-hashed, and one whose diff changed when
  a conflict was resolved. Measured cost: ~1-2s per worktree, scaling with how
  far the branch has drifted from the base, NOT with what the branch holds. A
  worktree 2251 commits behind main costs 2.1s on its own.
- **Cheap** (`reapNothingToLand` in internal/monitor/reap_worktrees.go):
  `git rev-list --count HEAD ^base ^<recorded landing>...`. One call, ~5ms.
  Cannot see a landing that was not recorded, so it over-reports outstanding
  work — safe for a delete decision, wrong for a display.

## What happened, and why this is filed

E-2087 replaced the SHA check with the exact one everywhere the two shared a
probe — including the worktree reaper. `monitor.ReapWorktreesForProject` is
called from FIVE branches of internal/hookcmd/claude.go, among them PreToolUse
and PostToolUse, so the reaper sweeps every worktree before and after every tool
call in every session. At ~90s per sweep that stopped the product, not just
`task spawn`.

The hotfix reverted the reaper to the cheap check and left the exact one on the
display surfaces (◆ in `session status`, `task unsettled`), which probe one row
or a handful rather than 139. The debt it accepted: a worktree whose work landed
under rewritten SHAs with no `task_landings` row reads as holding work forever,
so its directory is never reclaimed. That is the leak E-1940 and E-2087 each
tried to close, reopened deliberately because a slow leak is survivable and a
90-second tool call is not.

## What to decide

How to have the exact answer without paying for it per tool call. Directions
worth weighing, not a menu to pick from:

1. **Cache the verdict, keyed on (branch tip OID, base tip OID).** Both are
   ~1ms to read, and the key self-invalidates when either ref moves. The
   question is where it lives (a table? a file under the worktree's .git?) and
   what happens after a land, which moves the base and invalidates every entry
   at once — the cold sweep is back to ~90s unless something warms it.
2. **Take the reaper off the hook path.** A destructive background sweep
   running before and after every tool call is questionable independent of what
   it costs. Debounce it, run it on a timer, or move it to session start/end.
   This may be the real fix, with caching a nice-to-have on top.
3. **Make the exact answer cheaper.** The cost is dominated by patch-ids for
   every commit the base gained since the fork. Measured alternatives:
   `git cherry` (patch-id only) is ~3x faster but misses conflict-resolved
   landings; pairing by subject + author date is ~35x faster but disagrees with
   range-diff in BOTH directions, so it is unsafe alone. A union or a two-stage
   filter may be exact enough and much cheaper.
4. **Stop needing it.** ED-1587 makes branch names derivable and retires
   `task_landings.branch`. If landings were also recorded reliably, the cheap
   check would rarely be wrong — E-2087 measured worktrees whose work is on main
   with no landing row at all, and that recording gap is arguably the real
   defect underneath both leaks.

## Constraints any answer has to respect

- The reaper's mistakes are not symmetric. Refusing to reap costs disk; reaping
  a worktree that still holds work destroys it. Whatever it consults must be
  wrong only in the safe direction, or be exact.
- ◆, `task unsettled` and the reaper are supposed to agree about what "landed"
  means. The hotfix broke that on purpose and it should not stay broken.
- Whatever runs on the hook path is paid before and after every tool call.
  Budget it in milliseconds.

payload.title: Fix session resume refusing to self-resume the pane's own current task
payload.description: The guard that blocks session resume <id> when the pane already has a task variable assigned does not short-circuit when the resume target is that SAME task. Resume execs in place to avoid clobbering a different session, but self-resuming the pane current task clobbers nothing. It wrongly forces session goto --resume (new window) or --force. Expected: same-task self-resume proceeds without --force.

triage.rationale: The bug, root cause, and expected fix (short-circuit the guard when resume target equals the pane's current task) are all fully specified.

fields.analysis:
## Repro
In a tmux pane already bound to (working) E-1644, from the worktree:

    $ endless session resume E-1644 --db main
    Error: This pane is working E-1644. `session resume` execs in place, so it would replace that session.
      Open the target in a NEW window instead:
          endless session goto E-1644 --resume
      Or pass --force to replace this pane.

## Problem
`session resume` execs in place, so the guard refuses when the pane already has a task
variable assigned — to avoid clobbering a DIFFERENT live session in that pane. But when the
resume TARGET is the SAME task the pane already owns, there is no other session to protect:
resuming yourself replaces nothing meaningful (it is a re-enter of the task you are already on).
The guard should short-circuit that case instead of forcing `session goto --resume` (a new
window) or `--force`.

## Expected
When the pane's bound task == the resume target, `session resume <id>` proceeds without
`--force` — either a friendly no-op ("already here") or a clean re-enter/resume of the current
task. The replace-guard should fire ONLY when the pane's current task differs from the target.

## Fix location (starting point)
The `session resume` command's ownership/replace guard — the check that prints
"This pane is working E-<id>. `session resume` execs in place, so it would replace that
session." Add an equality short-circuit: if the current pane's bound task == the requested
target, bypass the "would replace that session" refusal. Confirm `session goto` and the
`--force` path stay unaffected.

## Verify
From a pane bound to task X: `endless session resume X` exits 0 (no `--force`) and does NOT
print the replace refusal; `endless session resume Y` (Y != X) still refuses without `--force`.

## Encountered
Hit live in session 6e7f46fb (the E-1644 worktree) on 2026-06-29 while trying to resume this
very task after it was completed.

payload.title: Stop recording a probe fault when git was killed by a signal
payload.description: A git probe killed by a signal is recorded as ERR-0010 worktree-probe-failed, so quitting `session monitor` with Ctrl-C leaves a permanent error incident naming a task that is fine. ## What was observed

2026-09-06 00:20:03 EDT, thirteen seconds after a land: incident 11,
`E-1972: git range-diff failed for its worktree`, detail
`git range-diff: signal: interrupt`. One occurrence.

The probe is healthy. `endless task unsettled E-1972` answers cleanly on
demand (unlanded, 7 commits), and a genuinely broken probe would not have
one occurrence — `session monitor` re-probes every row every two seconds
and the fault dedupes on (worktree, probe), so a real failure drives the
count into the thousands within a minute. The child git was KILLED, not
failed.

## Mechanism

`monitor.runGit` (internal/monitor/reap_worktrees.go) uses a plain
`exec.Command`, so the git child inherits the pane's foreground process
group. Ctrl-C to quit `session monitor` — routine after a land, since the
land replaces the global binary — reaches the in-flight git as well as the
monitor. Process table at the time confirms it: a monitor restarted at
00:19:57 and another at 00:20:04, bracketing the fault.

`worktreeUnsettledAt` (internal/monitor/worktree_unsettled.go) then applies
E-1940's fail-closed rule: any error from the probe means "this worktree
cannot be verified", which marks the row ◆ and calls `recordProbeFault`.
That rule cannot distinguish

  - git could not run (absent, broken repo, permissions) — a real incident, and
  - git was killed because its parent was interrupted — not an incident at all.

so a user quitting a view leaves a permanent error naming an innocent task.

## Fix direction

An `exec.ExitError` whose `ProcessState.Sys().(syscall.WaitStatus)` reports
`Signaled()` is not a probe failure. Return undetermined and record nothing:
the render is being torn down anyway, and nothing is left to display the ◆ to.
SIGINT and SIGTERM are the cases that matter; SIGKILL is ambiguous (an OOM kill
is arguably worth knowing about) and is worth a deliberate decision rather than
being swept in with the rest.

Worth deciding alongside: whether the probe should take a context, so an
interrupt CANCELS the sweep rather than racing it. Today each row's git is
killed independently and the loop keeps going, starting new children as it goes.

The FREQUENCY of this is a property of E-2111's cost problem — with
`git range-diff` on the display path, sampling `ps` once a second for ten
seconds found 4-6 of them in flight at every instant on this machine, so a
Ctrl-C lands on one with near-certainty. That measurement is recorded in

Any probe can be interrupted, including the cheap ones: making range-diff free
would shrink the window without closing it, and `git status --porcelain` sits
behind the same fail-closed rule.
